introduction: Xenophon, Apology 20–23; contextual comparison with Memorabilia 1.2.9–12. 350 Greek words in 7 paragraphs.

Based on Apology 20–23 with a separately labeled comparison to Memorabilia 1.2.9–12. Associations with Critias and Alcibiades are context, not substitute formal charges or proof of individual jurors’ motives. Reporting and perfect-system examples are course compositions.

Read once for the argument, then translate paragraph by paragraph. Attempt a complete first translation with uncertainties marked, consult glosses, then revise the sustained passage. Submit your connected English translation using the reading submission box.

The vocabulary panel separates new required entries from review words. Paragraph glosses supply additional reading support; a gloss alone does not make a word or an advanced construction a production requirement.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Σωκράτης ἐν τῇ τοῦ Ξενοφῶντος ἀπολογίᾳ περὶ τοῦ βίου μεγάλους λόγους λέγει. οὐ πάντες οἱ ἀκούοντες ἥδονται· τινὲς γὰρ θορυβοῦσιν. ὁ δὲ συγγραφεὺς ζητεῖ διὰ τί ὁ ἀνὴρ οὕτως εἴρηκεν. οὐκ ἀρκεῖ φάναι ὅτι οἱ δικασταὶ κακοὶ ἦσαν. δεῖ τὰ λεγόμενα, τὴν τοῦ λέγοντος γνώμην καὶ τὴν τῶν ἀκουόντων ἀπόκρισιν χωρὶς ἐξετάζειν.

Ὁ Σωκράτης τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἐλευθερίαν καὶ σωφροσύνην προβάλλει. τῶν γὰρ ἐπιθυμιῶν κεκρατηκέναι φησίν, καὶ οὐ χρήματα παρὰ τῶν συνόντων εἰληφέναι. ὅσα δὲ λέγει οἱ ἀκούοντες οὐ πάντες ὁμοίως δέχονται. ὁ μὲν νομίζει τοῦτο τεκμήριον ἀρετῆς εἶναι, ὁ δὲ μέμφεται τῇ μεγαληγορίᾳ. ἡ αὐτὴ φωνὴ δύναται διαφόρους κρίσεις κινεῖν.

Ἐν ἑτέρῳ δὲ βιβλίῳ, τοῖς Ἀπομνημονεύμασιν, ὁ Ξενοφῶν περὶ Κριτίου καὶ Ἀλκιβιάδου γράφει. οὗτοι τῷ Σωκράτει συνεγένοντο, ἔπειτα δὲ πολλὰ κακὰ τῇ πόλει ἐποίησαν. ὁ κατηγορῶν τὴν συνουσίαν αἰτίαν ποιεῖται· ὁ δὲ Ξενοφῶν ἀπολογεῖται καὶ ἐξετάζει πῶς ἐχρῶντο τῇ παιδείᾳ. οὐ τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον ἐν τοῖς δύο βιβλίοις ἀναγινώσκομεν.

Πρὸ τῆς δίκης ἡ πόλις πολλὰ πεπόνθει. πόλεμος καὶ ἧττα καὶ στάσις τοὺς πολίτας ἐβεβλάφεσαν. τινὲς φίλους ἀπολωλέκεσαν, ἄλλοι ἐκ τῆς πατρίδος ἔφυγον. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μνημονεύειν οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστι τῷ εἰδέναι τί ἕκαστος τῶν δικαστῶν ἐνόμιζεν. τὸ παρεληλυθὸς τὴν δίκην φωτίζει, οὐ μὴν ἀντὶ μαρτυρίας περὶ πάσης γνώμης ἐστίν.

Ἐρωτῶμεν οὖν τί ἴσμεν καὶ τί οἰόμεθα. οἶδα ὅτι ὁ Ξενοφῶν τοῦτο γέγραφεν· οὐκ οἶδα ὅτι πᾶς δικαστὴς διὰ τὴν αὐτὴν αἰτίαν ὠργίσθη. ἴσμεν τὰ ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ γεγραμμένα, ἀλλὰ δεῖ τὴν ἀπόδειξιν περὶ τοῦ πράγματος ζητεῖν. τὸ οἶδα μορφὴν παρακειμένου ἔχει, νῦν δὲ γνῶσιν δηλοῖ. τὸ δὲ ᾔδειν γνῶσιν ἐν παρελθόντι χρόνῳ.

Συγκρίνωμεν τρεῖς λόγους. ὁ κατήγορος εἶπεν· ὁ κατήγορος εἴρηκεν· ὁ κατήγορος ἤδη εἰρήκει πρὶν τὸν ἄλλον ἀποκρίνασθαι. ὁ μὲν πρῶτος τὴν πρᾶξιν διηγεῖται, ὁ δὲ δεύτερος τὸν εἰρημένον λόγον πρὸς τὸ νῦν συνάπτει, ὁ δὲ τρίτος πρὸς χρόνον ἤδη παρελθόντα. οὐ πᾶσα τοιαύτη διαφορὰ ἐν μιᾷ ἀγγλικῇ λέξει φαίνεται.

Ἡ δὲ δικαιοσύνη τῆς κρίσεως καὶ ἀκρίβειαν τῶν λόγων αἰτεῖ. ἄλλο «ὁ ἀνὴρ τούτοις συνῆν», ἄλλο «ὁ ἀνὴρ πάντα τὰ ἐκείνων ἔργα δεδίδαχεν». τὸ δεύτερον πλείω ἀπόδειξιν δεῖται. οὕτω καὶ τὸν Σωκράτη καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἀκούομεν, μὴ τὴν φιλίαν ἀντὶ τοῦ τεκμηρίου τιθέντες μηδὲ τὴν ὀργὴν ἀντὶ τοῦ λόγου.

reading.translation:
Socrates makes lofty claims about his life in Xenophon’s Apology. Not all the listeners are pleased: some make an uproar. The writer asks why the man has spoken this way. It is not enough to say that the jurors were bad. We must examine separately what was said, the speaker’s intention, and the listeners’ response.

Socrates puts forward his own freedom and moderation. He says that he has mastered his desires and has not taken money from his associates. The listeners do not all receive what he says in the same way. One considers it evidence of virtue; another criticizes the lofty speech. The same utterance can provoke different judgments.

In another work, the Memorabilia, Xenophon writes about Critias and Alcibiades. These two associated with Socrates and later did much harm to the city. The accuser makes their association an accusation; Xenophon defends Socrates and examines how they used their education. We are not reading the same argument in the two works.

Before the trial the city had suffered much. War, defeat, and civil conflict had harmed the citizens. Some had lost friends; others went into exile from their homeland. Remembering these things is not the same as knowing what each juror thought. The past illuminates the trial, but it is not testimony about every opinion.

We therefore ask what we know and what we suppose. I know that Xenophon has written this; I do not know that every juror became angry for the same reason. We know what is written in the book, but must seek evidence concerning the event. Oida has perfect form but expresses present knowledge. Ēidein expresses knowledge at a past time.

Let us compare three statements. The accuser spoke; the accuser has spoken; the accuser had already spoken before the other replied. The first narrates the act, the second connects the utterance with the present, and the third with a past reference time. Not every such difference appears in a single English word.

Justice in judgment also demands precision in statements. “The man associated with them” is one thing; “The man has taught all their actions” another. The second needs more evidence. In this way we listen both to Socrates and to his opponents, putting neither friendship in place of evidence nor anger in place of argument.

blocks.title: Knowing and supposing
body: Read these related expressions in the lesson’s argument. οἶδα means “know”; οἴομαι means “suppose”; τεκμήριον means “evidence”.
Explain which expression fits an action, a person, or an evaluation. A shared root connects meanings but does not make the words interchangeable in a sentence.

grammar.intro: II 28α–β. Original explanations and exercises follow the course grammar progression. Examples are teaching compositions, not additional ancient testimony. Complete each topic before the required grammar check.
objectives: Perfect and pluperfect active formation, including -κα and -α patterns and the assigned principal parts.
Reduplication, stem changes, common irregular forms, and the temporal relation of the pluperfect.
Active perfect aspect and its contrast with aorist narration and present states.
οἶδα and its assigned forms: perfect morphology with present meaning; distinguish knowing from having seen in translation.

sections.title: 1. Active perfects in -κα and -α
body: The active perfect often adds -κα to a reduplicated stem: λέλυκα, λέλυκας, λέλυκε(ν), λελύκαμεν, λελύκατε, λελύκασι(ν). The plural endings differ from present -ομεν/-ετε. Many verbs form a second perfect in -α with stem changes rather than -κα: γέγραφα, πέπομφα, πέπραχα, πέπονθα.

Principal parts identify these stems. Do not construct a perfect by attaching -κα indiscriminately: λαμβάνω → εἴληφα, λέγω → εἴρηκα, πάσχω → πέπονθα, γίγνομαι → γέγονα. Some perfects have strongly stative or intransitive senses. Form, lexical meaning, and context must be read together.

sections.title: 2. Active perfect participles and infinitives
body: The active perfect infinitive ends in -κέναι or the corresponding second-perfect ending: λελυκέναι, γεγραφέναι, εἰρηκέναι. In a report it can express completed prior action with present relevance. Keep it distinct from aorist λῦσαι and future λύσειν.

The participle has masculine -κώς, feminine -κυῖα, neuter -κός: λελυκώς, λελυκυῖα, λελυκός. The masculine/neuter stem appears in λελυκότος; the feminine uses first-declension endings, as λελυκυίας. Second perfects follow corresponding patterns, such as γεγραφώς, γεγραφυῖα, γεγραφός.

sections.title: 3. Active pluperfects
body: The pluperfect views a perfect state or completed action from a past point. Regular forms include ἐλελύκειν, ἐλελύκεις, ἐλελύκει, ἐλελύκεμεν, ἐλελύκετε, ἐλελύκεσαν; longer plural variants with -κει- also occur. The augment precedes the perfect stem when regularly expressed.

Irregular stems persist: ἐγεγράφει, “he had written”; ἐπεπόνθει, “he had suffered”; εἰρήκει, “he had said.” Initial-vowel and reduplication patterns mean that the past marker is not always a detachable ἐ-. Compare ἔγραψε, γέγραφε, and ἐγεγράφει by their time and aspect in a connected narrative.

sections.title: 4. οἶδα: perfect form, present knowledge
body: οἶδα is morphologically perfect but usually means “I know.” Learn οἶδα, οἶσθα, οἶδε(ν), ἴσμεν, ἴστε, ἴσασι(ν). Do not translate each occurrence “I have seen” simply because the form is historically connected with seeing. The infinitive is εἰδέναι and the participle εἰδώς, εἰδυῖα, εἰδός.

Past knowledge is expressed by pluperfect-shaped forms such as ᾔδειν, ᾔδεις, ᾔδει and plural ᾖσμεν/ᾔδεμεν, ᾖστε/ᾔδετε, ᾖσαν/ᾔδεσαν. Common nonindicatives include subjunctive εἰδῶ and optative εἰδείην. Distinguish “knows” from “supposes” and a claim to knowledge from evidence that supports it.

sections.title: 5. Aspect, evidence, and sequence
body: Compare an event, a current result, and an earlier result: εἶπεν, εἴρηκεν, εἰρήκει. English may sometimes render a Greek perfect with a simple present or past, but your analysis should retain the Greek viewpoint. “He has taught” emphasizes an action with relevance to the present assessment; “he taught” may simply advance a narrative.

In source analysis, do not let a perfect claim become stronger than its evidence. “They have associated with Socrates” and “Socrates has taught their crimes” are different propositions. Grammar can reveal what is being asserted, but cannot by itself establish the assertion’s truth.

table.title: 5. Aspect, evidence, and sequence
rows: He has spoken; perfect with present relevance.
He had spoken; prior result at a past viewpoint.
He knows; present state expressed by perfect-shaped form.

checks.prompt: Does a perfect tense prove the claim it expresses is true?
checks.answer: No; tense and evidence answer different questions.

checks.prompt: What is lost if every perfect is translated mechanically as “did long ago”?
checks.answer: Its resulting state or present relevance.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Apology
body: Xenophon’s Apology of Socrates is a short defense of the philosopher’s conduct at his trial in Athens in 399 BCE. “Apology” here means a defense, not an expression of regret. The work opens by asking why Socrates spoke with such elevated self-confidence. Xenophon wants the reader to understand the intention behind that manner, including Socrates’ judgment about his age, life, and approaching death. The choice of opening question shapes everything that follows.

The work moves from a conversation with Hermogenes before the trial to selected courtroom exchanges, reactions, the verdict, and Socrates’ response. It does not attempt to reproduce every procedural stage or every word spoken. Xenophon explicitly names Hermogenes as an informant in section 2. That is valuable evidence about a chain of testimony, but it does not turn the finished literary work into a transcript. Ask when the narrator summarizes, when Socrates answers an objection, and when a friend’s report supplies the connection.

Plato wrote a different Apology, and the two works should be read as distinct presentations. Do not silently import Plato’s famous phrases or penalty proposals into Xenophon’s account. Xenophon also defends Socrates across the four books of the Memorabilia, where conversations and habits provide a broader portrait. Read sections 1–9 for the preparation, 10–26 for the selected trial account, and the closing sections for the remembered aftermath. The complete translation linked here makes it possible to see the lesson’s excerpt in its argumentative setting. Across Lessons 45–47, notice how preparation, reputation, and courtroom reporting each illuminate a different part of Xenophon’s purpose.

sections.title: Claims that provoke reactions
body: In Xenophon’s Apology, Socrates’ elevated claims provoke noisy reactions. The author explains the manner as part of Socrates’ deliberate approach to his situation. An explanation of a speaker’s intention and a report of an audience’s reaction answer different questions.

Avoid drawing every juror as an irrational member of a single mob. We do not have access to each juror’s inner reasoning. The reading asks you to examine the speech and the narrator’s interpretation while acknowledging what the evidence does not reveal.

sections.title: Association is not an indictment
body: Memorabilia 1.2 discusses Critias and Alcibiades and their association with Socrates. That passage supplies a separate strand in Xenophon’s defense of his teacher. It must not be inserted into the Apology as if it were an additional formal charge preserved there.

Timeline: Arginusae was in 406 BCE; the Thirty and democratic restoration belong to 404–403; Socrates’ trial was in 399. Recent violence and political trauma are relevant context. They do not establish a single motive shared by every person who voted against him.

sections.title: Sort the claims
body: Create four headings: formal charge, association, narrator’s explanation, and conjecture. Place each statement you make about hostility toward Socrates under one heading and supply its source. If a claim fits more than one category, explain which part is documented and which is inferred.

Translate the pluperfect account of the city’s recent suffering, then the distinctions involving οἶδα. Finish with the last two paragraphs as a connected translation. Revise one overconfident claim by replacing certainty with the exact degree of support the source provides.

questions.prompt: What does association with Critias and Alcibiades establish by itself?
questions.answer: An association requiring analysis, not proof Socrates taught their crimes.

questions.prompt: Where does that comparison appear in the lesson’s sources?
How should claims about individual juror motives be handled?
questions.answer: With uncertainty unless evidence supports them.

Correct. οἶδα is morphologically perfect but usually means “I know.” Learn οἶδα, οἶσθα, οἶδε(ν), ἴσμεν, ἴστε, ἴσασι(ν). Do not translate each occurrence “I have seen” simply because the form is historically connected with seeing. The infinitive is εἰδέναι and the participle εἰδώς, εἰδυῖα, εἰδός.
